w: Named for the waterfall that still runs through its grounds, Kiyomizu-dera predates Kyoto itself -- one of only a few temples here older than the city's founding as Heian-kyo. Every December 12th its wooden stage hosts real theatre: a monk brush-paints the country's Kanji of the Year before the crowds.
s: A temple older than the city built around it
_facts: Buddhist temple in eastern Kyoto, full name Otowa-san Kiyomizu-dera; name means Pure Water Monastery
One of the few temples in Kyoto that predates the founding of the capital at Heian-kyo
Since 1995 has hosted the Kanji of the Year ceremony every 12 December
Part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto UNESCO World Heritage Site

w: The gold-leafed pavilion you see today is a rebuild: the original burned down in an arson attack, and the current structure went up in 1955 with its top two floors sheathed in gold leaf half a micron thick. Officially named Rokuon-ji, the Deer Garden Temple, it remains one of Kyoto's most photographed Zen sites.
s: A gilded pavilion rebuilt after an arson attack
_facts: Zen Buddhist temple officially named Rokuon-ji, the Deer Garden Temple
Nicknamed for its reliquary, the Golden Pavilion, whose top two floors are coated in 0.5-micron gold leaf
Current pavilion rebuilt in 1955 after being destroyed in an arson attack
Designated a World Heritage Site and National Special Historic Site

w: Founded in 711 by the Hata clan, an immigrant family from the Korean peninsula, this is the head shrine of Inari, kami of rice and, by extension, business. Merchants have donated torii gates ever since -- roughly 10,000 in total, some 800 packed tight enough to form the tunnel-like Senbon Torii up the mountain.
s: Ten thousand gates, each donated by a merchant
_facts: Head shrine of the kami Inari, founded 711 CE by the Hata clan
Sits at the base of Mount Inari; trails span about 4km and take roughly 2 hours to walk
Around 10,000 torii donated by businesses, about 800 forming the Senbon Torii tunnel

w: Saicho founded a monastery here in 788, on a peak ancient geomancers considered a shield against evil approaching Kyoto from the northeast. Enryaku-ji grew into a complex that trained nearly every major reformer of later Japanese Buddhism -- Honen, Nichiren, Dogen and Shinran all studied here first.
s: The mountain monastery that trained Japan's reformers
_facts: Mountain on the Kyoto-Shiga border; Enryaku-ji founded atop it by Saicho in 788, first outpost of the Tendai sect
Considered in ancient geomancy a protective bulwark against negative influences on Heian-kyo from the northeast
Later founders of major Japanese Buddhist schools -- Honen, Nichiren, Dogen, Shinran -- all trained here first

w: Built in the twilight of the Heian period in nearby Uji, Byodo-in belongs jointly to two Buddhist sects, the Pure Land Jodo-shu and the Tendai-shu -- a rare shared arrangement for a temple this old, and a quiet counterpoint to Kyoto's bigger-name pilgrimage sites.
s: A Heian-era temple shared by two Buddhist sects
_facts: Buddhist temple in Uji, Kyoto Prefecture, built in the late Heian period
Jointly belongs to the Jodo-shu (Pure Land) and Tendai-shu sects

w: Officially Jisho-ji, the Temple of Shining Mercy, this Zen temple in the Sakyo hills gave its 'Silver Pavilion' nickname to an entire aesthetic movement -- the Higashiyama Culture that shaped Muromachi-period taste in gardens, tea and architecture.
s: The temple that named an entire aesthetic era
_facts: Zen temple in the Sakyo ward of Kyoto, officially named Jisho-ji, the Temple of Shining Mercy
One of the constructions representing the Higashiyama Culture of the Muromachi period
